issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Failed Role: I have failed in my most important role in life
issues.explanation: For a 35-year-old single male special education teacher reporting a mugging/robbery, 'I have failed in my most important role in life' is hard to link coherently to the rest of the profile. The other appraisals center on self-blame and persistent danger, but this item implies a salient role failure theme (e.g. partner/parent/protector) that is not otherwise represented in triggers, threat, or memory.

issues.item: Memory: Shame on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense shame
issues.explanation: Within Memory, intense shame and intense rage on recall can coexist, but paired with a mugging/robbery and the rest of this profile they pull toward different meanings of the event without enough support elsewhere. Shame would usually connect to strong self-blame/humiliation themes, while rage would connect to injustice/anger themes; the profile does not integrate both clearly.

vignette: The rain had been heavy the night Julian Vance was cornered behind a row of parked cars, the mugger’s voice cracking into a sudden, piercing shout that froze him mid-step. Before Julian could react, the man’s hand clamped around the side of his neck, twisting just enough to send a sharp, lingering pain through his muscles that never quite faded. When the responding officers arrived, their radios crackled and their voices rose in urgent commands, compounding the disorientation until Julian’s hands shook on the steering wheel. That single afternoon left behind a constellation of alarms: the specific timbre of raised voices, the phantom tension in his throat, and the sight of uniformed authority figures. Over the following months, Julian found that any sudden shout—whether from a barking dog or a child’s tantrum down the street—did not simply startle him; it instantly pulled the night behind his eyes. He saw the encounter not as a fading dream, but as a series of still, high-definition frames locked in his mind. Looking at those silent images always brought a hot, crushing weight of rage for his own helplessness, followed immediately by a cold knot of guilt, as if the violence had somehow been his fault. Julian had come to believe that a competent adult would have de-escalated the situation or slipped away unnoticed, and this conviction that he was fundamentally inadequate seeped into how he processed every flashback, ensuring the guilt and rage only multiplied. At his Special Education classroom, where he spent his days mediating meltdowns and decoding nonverbal cues, this belief made it impossible for his shoulders to drop or his breathing to settle. Even when he locked his apartment door in the evening, the certainty that he was somehow defective kept his nervous system in a state of quiet emergency. He paced the perimeter of every room he entered, his eyes darting toward doorways and windows before he could even hang his coat, convinced that another attack would find him unprepared. The inability to relax soon began to rewrite his own perception. Because his body never truly disengaged from the perceived danger, the mind’s threat alarm grew overly sensitive, pulling the night’s memories into the present with startling frequency. When the photographic images flashed during a staff meeting or a grocery store aisle, the sudden physiological spike of threat forced him to scan the ceiling for exits, which in turn made him hyper-aware of any nearby shout or the distant wail of a patrol car siren. Each time his body braced for impact, the memories grew sharper, and the guilt and rage attached to them deepened. Julian’s constant hypervigilance and inability to unwind had convinced him that the world remained fundamentally hostile and that his own inadequacy was the reason he could never keep himself safe, which only kept him scanning for threats and waiting for the next trigger to strike. By spring, Julian’s classroom was quiet not because of better student management, but because he had stopped attending after-school programs to avoid the chaos of leaving groups and the occasional raised voice from the hallway. The exhaustion had become so profound that he finally sat in the intake room, his hands still resting lightly near the doorframe, and confessed that he was only there because he could no longer ignore the way his own mind had turned into a locked room. He hoped a therapist might help him quiet the permanent state of alert, though he feared that stopping his vigilance would mean failing to protect himself all over again.
